paras: The threatened lynching of William Butler occurred in New York City on October 4, 1903, after Butler, a Black man, was arrested for the fatal shooting of Dean Evans in a quarrel over a crap game. According to a wire dispatch, the policeman who caught Butler after chasing him in a commandeered electric car had to turn his revolver on an "immense crowd of excited men who wanted to lynch the prisoner." The two New York papers whose reports were found described the shooting and arrest but did not mention a crowd threat.

Butler, 23, of 449 Seventh Avenue, and Evans, a porter living at 328 West Thirty-seventh Street, were playing craps with other Black men, according to the New-York Tribune and the Sun. The Sun placed the game on a factory's steps at 343 West Thirty-seventh Street, during funerals for a murdered man and his killer in the same block. Accounts of the quarrel differed: the Tribune said Butler won a dollar and a dispute arose, the Sun said he lost a dollar to Evans and offered a torn bill that Evans refused, and the wire said he took the disputed stake and ran into the street.

In the Sun's version, Butler fired three shots that missed and fled toward Seventh Avenue with the players after him. Evans caught him in Thirty-sixth Street and tried to take the gun, and Butler fired twice at close range, hitting Evans in the leg and through the heart. The Tribune instead said Butler shot Evans in the forehead from an areaway on West Thirty-sixth Street, and that Butler told police he fired because Evans reached toward his hip pocket as if to draw a weapon. Evans died at the scene, and the Tribune reported that no weapon was found on his body.

The wire dispatch told a different story of the arrest: a policeman from the West Thirty-seventh Street station took possession of an electric car on Seventh Avenue, ran it at top speed for five blocks, and arrested Butler at the point of a revolver. After disarming Butler, the dispatch continued, the policeman was compelled to hold off a crowd that wanted to lynch him; the fuller version added that the streets were crowded with women and children and that there was "a panic in the neighborhood among the white persons who were witnesses of the killing." The Sun, by contrast, said that Butler had not gone far after the shooting when Policeman Flynn grabbed him.

The police said Butler confessed to the shooting. That afternoon friends of Evans passed a subscription paper around the block to pay for his burial; the Sun said he was unmarried and that his nearest relative was a brother. No report of an inquest, an indictment or a trial of Butler was found, and no member of the crowd was named or reported arrested.

The lynching claim reached readers outside New York through a wire dispatch dated October 5, printed that day in Minneapolis, Waterbury, Topeka, Providence, San Antonio and Butte. Most headlines featured the policeman's use of the streetcar, such as "Policeman Used a Car" and "Chased by Electric Car," while the Butte Inter Mountain added the deck "Lynching Nearly Averted." Later copies ran in the Duluth Labor World on October 10 and, as an item in a news-brief column, in the Wauwatosa News on October 17.

At home the case read as a local murder: the Tribune headlined it "Murder Ends Crap Game," and the Sun ran a feature-style account that called Evans "undersized but plucky" and closed with neighbors' talk rendered in dialect. Every white report identified the participants by race, the wire calling the shooting "the result of a dispute between negroes over a crap game." No report of the case in the Black press was found.

The lynching threat rests on the single wire dispatch, which names neither the policeman nor anyone in the crowd; the Tribune and the Sun, whose local accounts are more detailed, do not mention it, and the Sun's arrest on foot conflicts with the wire's streetcar chase. The papers also differ on the time of the shooting (early in the day in the Tribune, at noon in the Sun) and give Evans's first name as Dean or "Deery."

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Butler
bases: A wire dispatch says a crowd 'wanted to lynch' a Black prisoner arrested for murder and was held off by a policeman's revolver (A1, A2); no one was harmed by the crowd.

No one was killed by the crowd: Butler was arrested and held, and the only death was Evans's, by Butler's hand (A1, A3, A4). The crowd, an 'immense crowd' per the wire, wanted to lynch an accused murderer but was held at bay (A1, A2).

The killing and arrest are reported independently by the wire, the Tribune and the Sun (A1, A3, A4), but the lynching threat appears only in the one wire dispatch and its reprints; the local Tribune and Sun do not mention a crowd threat (A3, A4).

accounts.label: Wire report (New York, Oct. 5)
accounts.gist: A policeman ran a commandeered electric car five blocks to catch Butler, arrested him at revolver point, and then had to turn his revolver on an immense crowd that wanted to lynch him; Butler had taken the disputed stake and shot Evans when Evans grappled with him.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune (local)
accounts.gist: Butler won a dollar, a dispute arose, he ran into an areaway on West Thirty-sixth Street and shot Evans in the forehead, saying he thought Evans was drawing a weapon; no weapon was found on Evans. No crowd threat mentioned.

accounts.label: The Sun (local)
accounts.gist: Butler offered a torn bill for a dollar he lost, fired three wild shots, fled, and shot Evans twice when Evans caught him; Policeman Flynn grabbed him as he ran. No crowd threat or streetcar mentioned.

accounts.label: Butler's statement (via police)
accounts.gist: Butler confessed to the shooting but said he fired because Evans put his hand to his hip pocket as if to draw a knife or pistol.

framing.detail: Out-of-town papers ran the wire as a police-chase story ('Policeman Used a Car', 'Chased by Electric Car'), mentioning the would-be lynchers in one sentence; the Butte Inter Mountain added 'Lynching Nearly Averted'.
The Tribune reported a crap-game murder under 'Negro Who Won Dollar Shoots One of Pursuers', with no crowd threat.
The Sun wrote a feature-style account ('Little Negro Who'd Won Chased a Big Negro'), praising Evans as 'plucky' and ending with neighbors' talk rendered in mocking dialect; no crowd threat.
